findings.title: applyTemplateVariables called before $__range exclusion check
findings.body: The new code interpolates every query via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...)` before `partition(...)` runs `querySupportsSplitting`, which relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to exclude queries whose `$__range` would be interpolated on the backend with the split time range. After `applyTemplateVariables`, `$__range` is already replaced with the literal full-range value, so `isQueryWithRangeVariable` returns false and queries with `$__range` are now placed in the splitting path. The split sub-requests are then dispatched with the full-range literal inside the expression but a per-chunk time range, so each sub-query computes its rate over the wrong window and the merged result is incorrect. Before this PR the original `$__range` token was still present when `querySupportsSplitting` ran, so the exclusion worked; this PR silently bypasses it.

findings.title: Stale comment in querySupportsSplitting
findings.body: The comment above the `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` check says 'Queries with $__range variable should not be split because then the interpolated $__range variable is incorrect because it is interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange'. With the new `.map(applyTemplateVariables)` on line 296 running before `querySupportsSplitting`, that statement is no longer accurate: `$__range` is interpolated client-side first, so the check no longer protects against this scenario. Either the check needs to be performed before interpolation or the comment needs to be rewritten; right now the comment misleads readers about the actual control flow.

findings.title: No test covers $__range queries after early interpolation
findings.body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only exercises `$__auto` and `$step` and uses a `replace` mock that does not touch `$__range`. The most important behavior change in this PR is that `$__range` is now interpolated before `querySupportsSplitting` runs, but there is no test asserting that a `$__range`-bearing query is still routed to the non-splitting branch (or any test documenting the new behavior). Without such a test, the regression described in the other finding can re-occur unnoticed.

findings.title: No $__range test for shard splitting interpolation path
findings.body: The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts also only covers `$__auto` / `$step`. Since `runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` once on every target before sharding, the same `$__range` interpolation that happens client-side at this layer will propagate into the sub-requests `runSplitQuery` makes. A test that uses a `$__range` expression and asserts how the shard-selector and sub-request range interact would catch any future regression here.

findings.title: Mock for applyTemplateVariables mutates the input query
findings.body: Both beforeEach and the 'Sends the whole stream selector to fetch values' test install `datasource.applyTemplateVariables = jest.fn().mockImplementation((query) => { query.expr = query.expr.replace(...); return query; })`. The real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` returns a new query object (via `replaceQuery` / `templateSrv.replace`). Mocking it as a mutator can hide bugs where production code relies on the original `request.targets` being left untouched, because every other test sharing this setup will see `request.targets[i].expr` already rewritten. Consider mirroring production semantics in the mock (return a new object) so test behavior matches reality.
